title: Can AI chatbots plan a maths lesson?
author: Craig Barton
summary: This is the closing part of Craig Barton's three-part September 2024 test of what AI can do for teacher planning, and it tackles the hardest task: planning a whole lesson. After the general chatbots struggled, he turns to Oak National Academy's Aila, a free lesson assistant, and builds a Year 9 reverse-percentages lesson step by step, pushing it with follow-up prompts at each stage. Aila does well on prior-knowledge checks with follow-up questions, concrete examples of student misconceptions, and scripted teacher explanations, all of which teachers rarely have time to produce. It does badly on practice questions, fixating on answers of 100 pounds and ignoring requests to vary them, and its challenge questions lack real problem-solving. Barton's verdict is 'sort of': a real time-saver for an experienced teacher who can spot the deficiencies, but not a cure for lazy planning, and still unable to produce diagrams.
points: Aila's strongest output is the material teachers usually skip for lack of time, namely prior-knowledge checks with paired re-test questions, misconceptions illustrated by a child's likely words, and scripted explanations.

Its practice questions repeatedly gave 100 pounds as the answer, which lets students solve by inspection, and it claimed to fix this without changing anything, so a teacher still has to supplement with better sources.
The tool prompts for teacher input at every stage, but nothing forces that input, so a teacher can accept the first draft and the tool does not solve the problem of lazy planning.
Barton wonders how much expertise a teacher needs to notice what is wrong and prompt the fix, which makes the tool most valuable in experienced hands.
Diagram-dependent topics such as circle theorems come out with grey boxes or blank spaces, ruling out large areas of maths for now.
quotes: Lesson planning was the biggest consumer of my non-contact time for the first ten years of my teaching career. And the outputs of all that time spent were nothing to shout about.
Aila is not designed to do all the work for the teacher. It is a lesson planning assistant, and wants teacher input all along the way.
This is impressive. I can use these questions right away in the classroom to check how secure my students’ understanding is.

Having been messing about with these Chatbots for some time now, it is all too easy to get a bit blase about what is happening here. At the click of a button, I have a clear and concise explanation for how to solve reverse percentage problems.

But the practice questions are concerning. The obsession with £100 is something a competent teacher putting this lesson would never do, and it could have significant implications for students’ understanding.
The creation of diagrams seems like an insurmountable challenge at the moment, which rules out some significant areas of mathematics. But I am sure it will be solved soon.
